Trying to Conceive

Follitropin alfa: understanding your prescribed fertility treatment

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Follitropin alfa is a prescription fertility medicine that acts like follicle-stimulating hormone, usually shortened to FSH. It can help stimulate ovarian follicles or, in selected men, sperm production. Treatment is planned and monitored by a fertility specialist. The correct dose, injection device and storage instructions depend on the exact product and your treatment plan; one brand’s directions should not be applied automatically to another.

What follitropin alfa does

FSH is one of the hormones involved in reproductive function. It is normally released by the pituitary gland and works alongside other signals, including luteinising hormone, or LH. In the ovaries, FSH supports the growth of follicles that contain eggs. In the testes, it has a role in sperm production.

Follitropin alfa is a laboratory-produced form of FSH made using recombinant technology. Its purpose is to provide a controlled hormone signal when a clinician considers that useful for a particular fertility problem or assisted-reproduction treatment.

It is not a general fertility tonic, and a higher dose does not necessarily mean a better result. The response depends on the underlying condition, ovarian or testicular function and the other medicines in the programme.

Brand names, concentrations, vial contents and pen devices differ between markets. Check the active ingredient and the full product name with your clinic or pharmacist. A pen’s liquid volume is not a substitute for the prescribed number of international units, usually written as IU.

Why it may be prescribed for ovulation or assisted reproduction

One use is to help people who are not ovulating regularly. This may include selected people with polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, when other approaches have not produced the required response. Whether an oral treatment such as clomiphene or letrozole is tried first depends on the diagnosis and the clinic’s plan.

Another use is controlled ovarian stimulation during assisted reproduction. A clinic may use it to encourage follicle growth before a planned insemination or to develop several follicles before egg collection for IVF. The intended number of follicles and the acceptable response differ between these treatments.

People with a marked deficiency of both FSH and LH may need an LH-containing medicine as well. Follitropin alfa alone does not replace every missing hormone or every step in the reproductive process.

A separate medicine may be used to trigger final egg maturation or ovulation. The timing is part of the supervised protocol. Do not treat the daily FSH injection as interchangeable with a trigger injection or move either dose without advice.

Its role in selected male fertility treatment

Follitropin alfa can also be used for certain men with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, a condition in which the hormone signals needed for testicular function are insufficient. It is commonly combined with human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, in this setting.

The aim is to stimulate sperm production where the underlying problem is a lack of appropriate hormonal stimulation. That is different from treating every low sperm count, every semen abnormality or primary failure of the testes to respond.

Assessment and follow-up may include hormone measurements and semen testing. Treatment can take months, and the response is not immediate or guaranteed. A clinician should explain what improvement is being sought and how the plan will be reviewed.

It is misleading to describe this medicine as the best sperm booster for everyone. The diagnosis determines whether there is a reason to expect benefit and whether other investigations or treatments are needed.

What the clinic checks before treatment

The fertility team reviews the reason for treatment, medical history, other medicines and whether pregnancy would be medically appropriate. Depending on the situation, investigations may include reproductive hormone tests, ultrasound and assessment of both partners or gamete providers.

Certain conditions can make treatment inappropriate. These include allergy to the product, some pituitary or hypothalamic tumours, unexplained vaginal bleeding, and particular cancers of the ovary, uterus or breast. An ovarian cyst or enlargement of uncertain cause needs assessment; this is different from the ovarian appearance associated with PCOS.

Primary ovarian failure or primary testicular failure may mean that extra FSH will not produce the desired response. Some reproductive anatomical conditions also affect whether treatment can achieve a pregnancy. These are decisions for the specialist rather than conclusions to make from a symptom list.

Tell the team about thyroid or adrenal disease and other hormonal disorders so that untreated problems can be investigated and managed. Also discuss a history of blood clots, relevant family clotting history, heart or lung disease, asthma, and personal or family porphyria.

Not every condition in that history is an automatic contraindication. Some call for extra assessment, monitoring or a different plan. PCOS, in particular, is not a blanket reason that follitropin alfa can never be used; it can increase the risk of an excessive ovarian response.

Pregnancy, breastfeeding and other medicines

Follitropin alfa is used to support fertility treatment before pregnancy, not to maintain an established pregnancy. Tell your clinic if you may already be pregnant or receive a positive result during treatment. The verified product information does not indicate use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Give the clinic a complete list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, supplements and fertility products. Do not add leftover injections or medicines obtained from someone else, even if they appear to be part of a familiar protocol.

Other stimulation medicines can change the response. For example, hCG and clomiphene may increase ovarian stimulation, while medicines that suppress pituitary signalling can alter the FSH dose needed. A planned combination is not necessarily an unsafe interaction.

These combinations are deliberately selected and timed by the team. An interaction list should prompt a medication review, not an instruction to stop all other fertility medicines or to change the protocol yourself.

How monitoring guides the dose

The dose is individualised. Age, the reason for treatment, previous response and measures of ovarian reserve may influence the starting plan. During ovarian stimulation, ultrasound and sometimes blood tests help the clinic assess follicle growth and decide what should happen next.

Keep monitoring appointments even if you feel well. Symptoms alone cannot show how many follicles are developing or whether it is safe to proceed with a trigger injection, insemination or egg collection.

If the response is too strong, the team may change or stop injections, withhold a trigger or cancel a cycle. This can be disappointing, but it is intended to reduce complications. Ask for clear instructions about intercourse or contraception if too many follicles have developed.

Stimulation can increase the likelihood of more than one pregnancy in some settings. For IVF, embryo-transfer decisions also influence that risk. Discuss multiple pregnancy and other treatment risks before starting rather than assuming that more follicles always represent a better result.

Learning to give the injection safely

Use the exact device and route that have been prescribed. The GONAL-f products checked for this guide are given under the skin. That information does not justify switching a different product between subcutaneous and intramuscular injection or improvising a device technique.

A trained professional should show you how to prepare and administer your own product, select the prescribed dose and confirm that you understand the steps. If the pen, concentration or packaging changes, ask whether you need new instructions.

Follow the leaflet and clinic advice for hand hygiene, preparing the injection site, rotating sites and safe needle disposal. Use a fresh needle as directed and place used sharps in an appropriate container. Do not share a pen or needle.

The injection angle, preparation steps and any time allowed out of refrigeration depend on the device. Do not apply a universal ninety-degree rule, dilute a ready-to-use product, or calculate a volume from another brand’s instructions.

If a pen appears to jam, a dose may have leaked or you are unsure how much was delivered, contact the clinic or pharmacist. Guessing at a replacement dose can lead to receiving too much.

If a dose is late, missed or accidentally repeated

Contact the fertility clinic as soon as you realise that a dose has been missed. Tell them the product, prescribed dose, planned time and when the previous dose was taken. Their advice may depend on the point reached in the cycle and the other medicines being used.

Do not double a dose or automatically inject it as soon as you remember. The verified GONAL-f patient leaflet advises contacting the doctor after a missed dose. Your clinic should provide an out-of-hours contact or a written plan for timing problems.

If you accidentally use too much, contact the clinic promptly, even if you initially feel well. An excessive ovarian response can develop later. Severe pain, breathing problems, collapse or other emergency symptoms require urgent medical care rather than waiting for a callback.

Keeping a simple injection record can reduce uncertainty, especially when more than one medicine or person is involved. Record what was actually given, and leave decisions about corrective dosing to the clinical team.

Common discomforts and symptoms to report

Headache, local pain, redness, bruising or irritation at the injection site can occur. Abdominal discomfort, nausea and bloating are also reported during ovarian stimulation. Their significance depends on severity, progression and accompanying symptoms.

Breast tenderness or a change in bleeding may occur during a fertility cycle, but these do not reliably show whether treatment has worked or whether pregnancy has begun. Contact the clinic about unexpected vaginal bleeding rather than assuming every change is a harmless medicine effect.

New swelling in the hands, ankles or elsewhere should also be reported, especially if it is increasing or accompanies rapid weight gain, reduced urine or breathlessness. These symptoms should not be placed on a list of minor effects without explaining when they need review.

A symptom that is new, persistent or difficult to manage deserves advice even if it does not appear in a leaflet. Do not use a general article to decide that you must tolerate worsening pain until the next scheduled scan.

Recognising ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, or OHSS, is an excessive response to ovarian stimulation. The ovaries enlarge and fluid can move out of blood vessels into other parts of the body. It can begin during treatment or develop after injections have stopped, particularly around subsequent hormonal changes or pregnancy.

Milder symptoms can include bloating and abdominal discomfort. Increasing abdominal swelling or pain, repeated vomiting, marked thirst, rapid weight gain or passing less urine require prompt contact with the fertility unit. Severe OHSS can affect breathing and circulation and may need hospital care.

Seek emergency help for difficulty breathing, chest pain, collapse or severe symptoms. Do not dismiss them because the last injection was several days ago. PCOS, a previous episode and a strong ovarian response are among the factors the team considers when assessing risk.

Follow the clinic’s instructions about activity, intercourse and follow-up if the ovaries are enlarged or OHSS is suspected. Do not try to manage a worsening case simply by drinking more water or taking extra painkillers without assessment.

Other uncommon but serious warning signs

A severe allergic reaction can cause hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, wheezing, difficulty breathing or faintness. Seek emergency care immediately. A mild local injection reaction does not look or behave the same as a reaction affecting breathing or circulation.

Blood clots are uncommon but can be serious, with or without OHSS. Sudden chest pain, breathlessness, a painful swollen limb, or symptoms such as one-sided weakness, difficulty speaking, new confusion or sudden visual disturbance need emergency assessment.

Chest pressure extending to the jaw or arm should also be treated urgently. These are not ordinary fertility-treatment discomforts to watch at home. Explain that you are receiving ovarian-stimulation treatment when seeking help.

A suddenly severe, particularly one-sided lower abdominal pain may need urgent assessment for ovarian torsion or another acute problem. The cause cannot be established at home. Asthma worsening or a suspected porphyria flare also needs prompt advice from the treating team.

Storage and checking the medicine before use

Read the storage instructions for your exact product, strength and presentation. Some follitropin alfa products are refrigerated pens; others are powders with different storage and preparation requirements. A rule about keeping every product in the refrigerator for four weeks after opening is not reliable.

The checked GONAL-f multidose pen leaflet includes refrigeration and a limited period of use after opening, while the checked powder product is intended for use immediately after reconstitution. These examples show why a shared active ingredient does not mean identical storage instructions.

Ask your pharmacist about transport, travel, a refrigerator failure or an uncertain temperature exposure. Follow the product’s limits on heat, freezing and light. Do not warm an injection using hot water, a microwave or direct heat.

Check the expiry date and any written opening or preparation date. Do not use a solution that looks wrong for the product, contains unexpected particles or has damaged packaging; ask a pharmacist. Keep medicines and sharps away from children and arrange safe disposal of unused supplies.

What the treatment does not tell you

Follitropin alfa does not reliably select a baby’s sex. Describing an FSH injection as a way to have a boy confuses ovarian stimulation with entirely different questions about reproduction and genetic testing.

Changes in period timing, flow or duration also do not prove success or failure. Follow the clinic’s pregnancy-testing timetable and report bleeding that is unusually heavy, persistent or associated with severe pain, dizziness or faintness.

The most useful questions are practical: what is this medicine intended to do in my case, how will the response be checked, what should I do if a dose goes wrong, and whom can I contact after hours? Have those answers available before beginning the injections.

This information can support that conversation, but the prescription and the instructions for the product in your hand remain essential. Do not change the dose, route or treatment schedule on the basis of a general article.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Regulated product information describes follitropin alfa’s uses, contraindications, monitoring and adverse effects. PCOS can be a reason for treatment in selected cases, while also increasing the risk of an excessive ovarian response.

Product instructions differ between powders, pens and brands. The independent references below support the active-ingredient discussion and OHSS advice; they do not establish the instructions for every locally available product.

How BeMama can help

Before starting, keep your prescription, exact product leaflet, injection record and clinic contact details together. Ask the team to explain any difference between the leaflet and your individual treatment plan.

When to seek help

Do not double a missed dose or transfer injection and storage directions from another brand. Contact your clinic for worsening abdominal symptoms and seek emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest symptoms, stroke-like signs or a severe allergic reaction.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Follitropin alfa supplies an FSH signal for selected fertility treatments; it is not a universal fertility or sperm booster.
  • Ultrasound and other monitoring guide treatment; do not change doses or skip appointments on the basis of symptoms alone.
  • PCOS is not a blanket contraindication, but it can increase the risk of OHSS.
  • Missed doses, injection technique and storage need advice for the exact prescribed product.
  • Severe abdominal symptoms, breathing problems, chest pain, neurological symptoms or allergy signs need urgent help.

Frequently asked questions

Is follitropin alfa the same as a trigger injection?

No. It supports follicle growth. A separate medicine may be used for final egg maturation or ovulation, depending on the protocol. Use each medicine at the time and dose specified by your clinic.

Can someone with PCOS use this medicine?

Sometimes. PCOS is not an automatic contraindication, and selected patients may receive FSH treatment. Because an excessive ovarian response is more likely in some people with PCOS, careful dose selection and monitoring are important.

Can it improve every low sperm count?

No. Its established role includes selected men whose sperm production is affected by insufficient reproductive hormone signals, commonly alongside hCG. Other causes of low sperm count may require a different approach.

Should I take a forgotten injection immediately?

Contact your clinic promptly for instructions. Do not automatically take it late or double the next dose. Timing advice depends on your protocol, and the verified patient leaflet directs you to speak to the doctor after a missed dose.

Can OHSS start after the injections have stopped?

Yes. Symptoms can develop or worsen afterwards, particularly around trigger treatment or pregnancy. Increasing abdominal pain or swelling, repeated vomiting, rapid weight gain or reduced urine needs prompt advice; breathing difficulty or chest symptoms need emergency care.

Does every pen need the same storage conditions?

No. Limits differ by product and presentation, including before and after opening. Use your own leaflet and ask a pharmacist about temperature exposure, travel or an uncertain expiry. Do not transfer a four-week rule from another brand.

Can I use the same injection technique for a vial and a pen?

Not automatically. Preparation, dose selection and device steps can differ. Ask for training for the product you have and do not change between injection routes without the prescriber’s instructions.

Does a change in bleeding mean that I am pregnant?

No. Timing and flow can change during treatment for several reasons. Follow the clinic’s testing schedule and report unexpected bleeding. Heavy bleeding with severe pain, faintness or dizziness needs urgent assessment.

Will the injections increase the chance of having a boy?

Follitropin alfa is not a reliable method of sex selection. Its role is reproductive hormone stimulation, not choosing a baby’s sex.

What if I am unsure whether the full dose went in?

Contact the clinic or pharmacist and describe what happened, including the device and displayed dose. Do not guess at a top-up injection. A written dose record and access to an out-of-hours contact can help prevent an accidental repeat.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
